title: JSON Merge Patch
summary: This specification defines the JSON merge patch format and processing rules, primarily for use with the HTTP PATCH method to describe changes to a target resource's content. It replaces RFC 7386.

plainLanguage.summary: If you only need to fix a few fields in a big form, send just those fields. This RFC defines a simple way to describe those changes for JSON.

questions: remove a field with merge patch
how to remove a field with merge patch
subtitle: Describe a change to a JSON document by sending a small document that looks like the part you want changed.

tldr.problem: Changing part of a JSON resource over HTTP PATCH needs a compact way to say what to change without resending the whole document.
tldr.mechanism: A merge patch is a JSON document that mimics the target. Members in the patch are added or replaced, and members set to null are removed, following the MergePatch function.
tldr.outcome: It is simple, but it cannot patch part of an array or set a member to an explicit null. This document obsoletes RFC 7386.

today: RFC 7396 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7386. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Merge Patch Idea
sections.content:
This specification defines the JSON merge patch document format, its processing rules, and the media type application/merge-patch+json. It is primarily intended for the HTTP PATCH method (RFC 5789) as a way to describe modifications to a target resource's content.

A patch uses a syntax that closely mimics the document being modified. The recipient compares the patch with the current target. Members missing from the target are added, members already present are replaced, and null values mean removal of existing values.
sections.plainLanguage: To fix a typo on a form, you do not rewrite the whole form. You hand back a note with only the fields that change.

sections.title: The MergePatch Function
sections.content:
The RFC defines the effect of a pseudocode function MergePatch(Target, Patch). If the patch is an object, a non-object target is first replaced with an empty object. Then for each name and value in the patch: a null value removes the name from the target if it exists, and any other value is merged in recursively. If the patch is not an object, the result is the patch itself.

Two consequences follow. A patch that is not an object replaces the entire target. And it is not possible to patch part of a non-object target, such as replacing just some values in an array.

The operation works on data items, not text, so it need not preserve white space, member ordering or number precision beyond what the target implementation has. If an object has multiple members with the same name, the result is not defined.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is: if your note is a list of fields, update each one, and a blank means throw that field away. If your note is anything else, it simply replaces everything.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
Given a document with title 'Goodbye!', an author object with givenName and familyName, a tags array of 'example' and 'sample', and a content member, a client sends a PATCH with Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json. The patch changes title to 'Hello!', adds phoneNumber, sets author.familyName to null, and supplies tags as [ "example" ].

The result keeps givenName and content untouched, drops familyName, and the whole tags array is replaced rather than edited. Appendix A lists more test cases, including patches that are arrays or null.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a note saying 'new title, add a phone number, remove the last name, and here is the full new tag list'. Everything you did not mention stays as it was.

sections.title: Where It Does Not Fit
sections.content:
Because null means removal, merge patch suits JSON documents that mostly use objects and do not make use of explicit null values. The RFC says the format is not appropriate for all JSON syntaxes. Arrays can only be replaced as a whole.

The test cases show the edge cases: patching {"e":null} with {"a":1} keeps the null member, and patching the array [1,2] with an object produces an object with only the non-null members.
sections.plainLanguage: This works best when your data is made of named fields. It is awkward for lists, and it cannot store 'nothing' as a value, because 'nothing' means 'remove'.

sections.title: The Media Type
sections.content: The RFC registers the media type application/merge-patch+json with no required or optional parameters. Resources using it must conform to application/json and so follow the same encoding considerations as RFC 7159. The intended usage is COMMON and the change controller is the IESG.
sections.plainLanguage: It gets an official label, so a server can tell that this note is a merge patch and not a plain document.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The media type lets a client indicate that the server should work out the specific changes to apply. It is therefore the server's responsibility to decide whether each change is appropriate and whether the client is authorized to request it. How is out of scope for this specification.

All of the security considerations in Section 5 of RFC 5789 apply to every use of HTTP PATCH with this media type.
sections.plainLanguage: The server decides what changes are allowed and who may ask for them. A note saying 'change this' is a request, not an order.
